cards.front: What is the agentic loop lifecycle in Claude-based systems?
cards.back: Send request → inspect stop_reason → if tool_use, execute tools and append results to history → repeat until stop_reason is end_turn.
sources: Official CCAR-F Exam Guide — D1, Task 1.1
https://docs.anthropic.com/en/docs/agents-and-tools/agent-sdk/overview

cards.front: 12% of support cases skip get_customer and call lookup_order by name only, causing wrong refunds. Most effective fix?
cards.back: Programmatic prerequisite: block lookup_order and process_refund until get_customer returns a verified customer ID.
cards.rationale: Financial identity steps need deterministic enforcement; prompts and few-shot alone are probabilistic.
sources: Official CCAR-F Exam Guide — D1, Task 1.4; Sample Q1

cards.front: Single agent with many tools vs coordinator + specialized subagents for a research pipeline?
cards.back: Coordinator + subagents when work decomposes (search, analyze, synthesize), needs isolated context, and clear failure boundaries.
sources: Official CCAR-F Exam Guide — D1, Task 1.2

cards.front: Why must a coordinator not invent subagent outputs without tool results?
cards.back: Breaks provenance and reliability; delegate via Task tool and pass explicit context—never hallucinate worker findings.
sources: Official CCAR-F Exam Guide — D1, Task 1.2–1.3

cards.front: When should an agentic loop continue vs terminate?
cards.back: Continue when stop_reason is tool_use; terminate when stop_reason is end_turn.
sources: Official CCAR-F Exam Guide — D1, Task 1.1

cards.front: Agentic loop anti-patterns for termination (name three).
cards.back: Parsing natural language for completion; arbitrary iteration caps as primary stop; treating assistant text as completion signal.
sources: Official CCAR-F Exam Guide — D1, Task 1.1

cards.front: Model-driven tool selection vs pre-configured decision trees?
cards.back: Model-driven: Claude picks tools from context each turn. Decision trees/forced sequences bypass model reasoning—use only when deterministic ordering is required.
sources: Official CCAR-F Exam Guide — D1, Task 1.1

cards.front: Why append tool results to conversation history between loop iterations?
cards.back: So the model can reason about new information and choose the next action based on actual tool output.
sources: Official CCAR-F Exam Guide — D1, Task 1.1

cards.front: What is hub-and-spoke multi-agent architecture?
cards.back: Coordinator manages all inter-subagent communication, error handling, and information routing; subagents do not talk directly.
sources: Official CCAR-F Exam Guide — D1, Task 1.2

cards.front: Do subagents automatically inherit the coordinator's conversation history?
cards.back: No—subagents operate with isolated context; parent history is not inherited automatically.
sources: Official CCAR-F Exam Guide — D1, Task 1.2–1.3

cards.front: Research on 'AI in creative industries' covers only visual arts—logs show coordinator assigned digital art, graphic design, photography only. Root cause?
cards.back: Coordinator task decomposition too narrow—subagents executed correctly but were assigned incomplete scope.
sources: Official CCAR-F Exam Guide — D1, Task 1.2; Sample Q7

cards.front: How should a coordinator select which subagents to invoke?
cards.back: Analyze query requirements and dynamically select needed subagents—not always route through the full pipeline.
sources: Official CCAR-F Exam Guide — D1, Task 1.2

cards.front: How partition research scope across subagents to reduce duplication?
cards.back: Assign distinct subtopics or source types per agent (e.g., web vs documents vs synthesis)—not overlapping queries.
sources: Official CCAR-F Exam Guide — D1, Task 1.2

cards.front: What is an iterative refinement loop in multi-agent research?
cards.back: Coordinator evaluates synthesis for gaps, re-delegates to search/analysis with targeted queries, re-invokes synthesis until coverage is sufficient.
sources: Official CCAR-F Exam Guide — D1, Task 1.2

cards.front: Why route all subagent communication through the coordinator?
cards.back: Observability, consistent error handling, and controlled information flow.
sources: Official CCAR-F Exam Guide — D1, Task 1.2

cards.front: What tool spawns subagents in the Agent SDK, and what must allowedTools include?
cards.back: The Task tool; allowedTools must include "Task" for a coordinator to invoke subagents.
sources: Official CCAR-F Exam Guide — D1, Task 1.3

cards.front: How pass prior agent findings to a synthesis subagent?
cards.back: Include complete findings directly in the subagent prompt (search results, document analysis)—not rely on automatic inheritance.
sources: Official CCAR-F Exam Guide — D1, Task 1.3

cards.front: Best practice when passing context between agents for attribution?
cards.back: Use structured formats separating content from metadata (URLs, document names, page numbers).
sources: Official CCAR-F Exam Guide — D1, Task 1.3

cards.front: How spawn parallel subagents for lower latency?
cards.back: Emit multiple Task tool calls in a single coordinator response—not separate turns per subagent.
sources: Official CCAR-F Exam Guide — D1, Task 1.3

cards.front: Coordinator prompts: step-by-step procedures vs research goals?
cards.back: Specify research goals and quality criteria—enables subagent adaptability vs rigid procedural scripts.
sources: Official CCAR-F Exam Guide — D1, Task 1.3

cards.front: What does AgentDefinition configure for each subagent type?
cards.back: Description, system prompt, and tool restrictions per subagent role.
sources: Official CCAR-F Exam Guide — D1, Task 1.3

cards.front: What is fork-based session management in multi-agent workflows?
cards.back: Create independent branches from a shared analysis baseline to explore divergent approaches (e.g., two testing strategies).
sources: Official CCAR-F Exam Guide — D1, Task 1.3, 1.7

cards.front: Programmatic enforcement (hooks, gates) vs prompt-based workflow ordering?
cards.back: Prompts have non-zero failure rate; programmatic gates give deterministic compliance when identity verification or financial ops require it.
sources: Official CCAR-F Exam Guide — D1, Task 1.4

cards.front: Customer message has multiple concerns (billing + return). How should the agent investigate?
cards.back: Decompose into distinct items, investigate each in parallel using shared context, then synthesize a unified resolution.
sources: Official CCAR-F Exam Guide — D1, Task 1.4

cards.front: What must a structured human handoff include when escalating mid-process?
cards.back: Customer details, root cause analysis, recommended actions—humans may lack full conversation transcript.
sources: Official CCAR-F Exam Guide — D1, Task 1.4

cards.front: Example structured handoff fields for a refund escalation?
cards.back: Customer ID, root cause, refund amount, recommended action.
sources: Official CCAR-F Exam Guide — D1, Task 1.4

cards.front: PostToolUse hook—what does it do?
cards.back: Intercepts tool results after execution to transform/normalize data before the model processes them.
sources: Official CCAR-F Exam Guide — D1, Task 1.5

cards.front: MCP tools return mixed timestamp formats (Unix, ISO 8601). Best approach before agent reasoning?
cards.back: PostToolUse hook to normalize heterogeneous formats into a consistent representation.
sources: Official CCAR-F Exam Guide — D1, Task 1.5

cards.front: Business rule: block refunds over $500 and escalate. Hooks vs prompt instructions?
cards.back: Tool call interception hook—hooks guarantee compliance; prompts are probabilistic.
sources: Official CCAR-F Exam Guide — D1, Task 1.5

cards.front: Tool call interception hooks—purpose?
cards.back: Block policy-violating outgoing tool calls (e.g., large refunds) and redirect to alternative workflows (human escalation).
sources: Official CCAR-F Exam Guide — D1, Task 1.5

cards.front: Fixed sequential pipeline (prompt chaining) vs dynamic adaptive decomposition?
cards.back: Sequential pipelines for predictable multi-step reviews; dynamic decomposition for open-ended investigation that adapts to intermediate findings.
sources: Official CCAR-F Exam Guide — D1, Task 1.6

cards.front: 14-file PR review misses bugs and gives contradictory feedback. Restructure approach?
cards.back: Per-file local analysis passes, then a separate cross-file integration pass—avoids attention dilution.
sources: Official CCAR-F Exam Guide — D1, Task 1.6; Sample Q12

cards.front: Task: add comprehensive tests to a legacy codebase. Decomposition strategy?
cards.back: Map structure → identify high-impact areas → prioritized plan that adapts as dependencies are discovered.
sources: Official CCAR-F Exam Guide — D1, Task 1.6

cards.front: What is prompt chaining for task decomposition?
cards.back: Break work into sequential focused steps (e.g., analyze each file, then cross-file integration pass).
sources: Official CCAR-F Exam Guide — D1, Task 1.6

cards.front: Named session resumption in Claude Code—how?
cards.back: Use --resume with a session name to continue a specific prior conversation.
sources: Official CCAR-F Exam Guide — D1, Task 1.7

cards.front: What is fork_session used for?
cards.back: Create parallel exploration branches from a shared baseline (e.g., compare two refactoring or testing strategies).
sources: Official CCAR-F Exam Guide — D1, Task 1.7

cards.front: Resume session after code changed vs start fresh?
cards.back: Resume when prior context is mostly valid; start fresh with injected summary when prior tool results are stale—more reliable than stale resumes.
sources: Official CCAR-F Exam Guide — D1, Task 1.7

cards.front: Resuming a session after specific files changed—what to tell the agent?
cards.back: Inform about specific file changes for targeted re-analysis—not require full re-exploration of the codebase.
sources: Official CCAR-F Exam Guide — D1, Task 1.7

cards.front: Synthesis needs simple fact-checks (85%) but complex search (15%). Reduce latency without over-provisioning?
cards.back: Give synthesis a scoped verify_fact tool for simple lookups; complex verifications still delegate through coordinator to search agent.
sources: Official CCAR-F Exam Guide — D1, Task 1.2–1.3; Sample Q9

cards.front: Customer Support and Multi-Agent Research scenarios—shared primary domain?
cards.back: D1 (Agentic Architecture & Orchestration)—plus D2 tools/MCP and D5 context/reliability for both.
sources: Official CCAR-F Exam Guide — scenario map

cards.front: Four coordinator responsibilities in hub-and-spoke orchestration?
cards.back: Task decomposition, delegation to subagents, result aggregation, and dynamic selection of which subagents to invoke.
sources: Official CCAR-F Exam Guide — D1, Task 1.2

cards.front: Do subagents share memory across separate Task invocations?
cards.back: No—each invocation is isolated; context must be explicitly provided in the prompt every time.
sources: Official CCAR-F Exam Guide — D1, Task 1.3

cards.front: What is attention dilution in multi-step agent workflows?
cards.back: Processing too many items in one pass (many files, broad topics) reduces depth and consistency—some areas get superficial treatment while others are detailed.
sources: Official CCAR-F Exam Guide — D1, Task 1.6

cards.front: What is an adaptive investigation plan for task decomposition?
cards.back: Generate subtasks based on what is discovered at each step—not a fixed pipeline decided upfront.
sources: Official CCAR-F Exam Guide — D1, Task 1.6

cards.front: PostToolUse hook: what heterogeneous MCP fields should you normalize before the model sees them?
cards.back: Timestamps (Unix vs ISO 8601), numeric status codes, and other inconsistent formats from different backend tools.
sources: Official CCAR-F Exam Guide — D1, Task 1.5

cards.front: Web search subagent times out. Best error propagation to the coordinator?
cards.back: Structured error context: failure type, attempted query, partial results, and potential alternative approaches.
sources: Official CCAR-F Exam Guide — D1, Task 1.2; Sample Q8

cards.front: Agent skips identity verification before refunds. Why is a routing classifier the wrong first fix?
cards.back: Problem is tool ordering, not tool availability—a classifier limits which tools exist but does not enforce get_customer before lookup_order/refund.
sources: Official CCAR-F Exam Guide — D1, Task 1.4; Sample Q1

cards.front: When should a support agent escalate to a human instead of continuing the agentic loop?
cards.back: Policy requires human judgment, identity cannot be verified, tool failures persist, or validation/confidence thresholds are not met.
sources: Official CCAR-F Exam Guide — D1; Customer Support scenario

cards.front: Developer Productivity scenario—primary domains and D1 focus?
cards.back: D2 (tools/MCP), D3 (Claude Code), D1 (delegation/orchestration with built-in tools + MCP servers).
sources: Official CCAR-F Exam Guide — scenario map

cards.front: Typical subagent roles in a multi-agent research pipeline (Exam Scenario 3)?
cards.back: Web search, document analysis, synthesis of findings, and report generation—coordinator delegates each role.
sources: Official CCAR-F Exam Guide — Scenario 3; D1, Task 1.2

cards.front: Subagent catches timeout and returns empty results marked successful. Why wrong?
cards.back: Suppresses failure—coordinator cannot recover, retry, or annotate coverage gaps; risks incomplete research output.
sources: Official CCAR-F Exam Guide — D1; Sample Q8

cards.front: Subagent timeout propagates and terminates the entire research workflow. Why wrong?
cards.back: Single failures often recoverable with partial results, alternate queries, or gap annotation—unnecessary full termination.
sources: Official CCAR-F Exam Guide — D1; Sample Q8

cards.front: When is prompt-based workflow guidance enough vs requiring programmatic gates or hooks?
cards.back: Prompts suffice for soft ordering and preferences; programmatic enforcement when business rules need deterministic compliance (identity before money, refund caps).
sources: Official CCAR-F Exam Guide — D1, Task 1.4–1.5

cards.front: Subagent retries timeout internally then returns generic 'search unavailable' to coordinator. Gap?
cards.back: Hides failure type, attempted query, and partial results—coordinator cannot make informed recovery decisions.
sources: Official CCAR-F Exam Guide — D1; Sample Q8

cards.front: Two stop_reason values that drive agentic loop control?
cards.back: tool_use (continue loop—execute tools and append results) and end_turn (terminate and present response).
sources: Official CCAR-F Exam Guide — D1, Task 1.1; Appendix

cards.front: Give synthesis agent all web search tools to eliminate coordinator round-trips. Why avoid?
cards.back: Over-provisions synthesis—violates separation of concerns and role-specific tool scoping; use scoped tools for common cases only.
sources: Official CCAR-F Exam Guide — D1; Sample Q9

cards.front: What is a programmatic prerequisite gate in a multi-step agent workflow?
cards.back: Code or hook that blocks downstream tool calls until a prerequisite step completes (e.g., no refund until verified customer ID).
sources: Official CCAR-F Exam Guide — D1, Task 1.4

cards.front: What does MCP (Model Context Protocol) provide to Claude agents?
cards.back: A standard way for AI clients to discover and invoke tools, resources, and prompts from external servers.
sources: Official CCAR-F Exam Guide — D2
https://modelcontextprotocol.io/introduction

cards.front: Primary mechanism LLMs use to select among similar tools?
cards.back: Tool descriptions—minimal descriptions lead to unreliable selection when tools overlap.
sources: Official CCAR-F Exam Guide — D2, Task 2.1

cards.front: Agent calls get_customer for order queries (#12345) instead of lookup_order. Both have minimal descriptions. Best first fix?
cards.back: Expand each tool description: input formats, example queries, edge cases, and when to use vs similar tools.
cards.rationale: Descriptions are the primary selection mechanism; few-shot and routing layers don't fix inadequate descriptions first.
sources: Official CCAR-F Exam Guide — D2, Task 2.1; Sample Q2

cards.front: What should effective tool descriptions include beyond a one-line summary?
cards.back: Expected inputs, outputs, example queries, edge cases, and boundaries explaining when to use vs similar alternatives.
sources: Official CCAR-F Exam Guide — D2, Task 2.1

cards.front: analyze_content and analyze_document have near-identical descriptions. Likely result?
cards.back: Tool misrouting—the model cannot reliably distinguish overlapping tools with ambiguous descriptions.
sources: Official CCAR-F Exam Guide — D2, Task 2.1

cards.front: Generic analyze_content overlaps with analyze_document. Rename/fix strategy?
cards.back: Rename to purpose-specific names (e.g., extract_web_results) with web-specific descriptions that eliminate overlap.
sources: Official CCAR-F Exam Guide — D2, Task 2.1

cards.front: One generic analyze_document tool does too much. How split it?
cards.back: Purpose-specific tools with clear contracts: extract_data_points, summarize_content, verify_claim_against_source.
sources: Official CCAR-F Exam Guide — D2, Task 2.1

cards.front: How can system prompt wording undermine well-written tool descriptions?
cards.back: Keyword-sensitive instructions can create unintended tool associations that override description clarity.
sources: Official CCAR-F Exam Guide — D2, Task 2.1

cards.front: Tool selection still wrong after improving descriptions. Next check?
cards.back: Review system prompt for keyword-sensitive instructions that might override tool descriptions.
sources: Official CCAR-F Exam Guide — D2, Task 2.1

cards.front: Why expose one mega-tool that 'does anything on GitHub' to the agent?
cards.back: Harder correct selection, weak error semantics, and excessive blast radius if mis-invoked.
sources: Official CCAR-F Exam Guide — D2, Task 2.1

cards.front: Similar tools misroute. Why is consolidating into lookup_entity not the best first step?
cards.back: Valid architecture but higher effort; immediate problem is inadequate descriptions—expand those first (Sample Q2).
sources: Official CCAR-F Exam Guide — D2, Task 2.1; Sample Q2

cards.front: MCP pattern for communicating tool failures back to the agent?
cards.back: The isError flag on tool results, plus structured error metadata—not raw stack traces or generic messages.
sources: Official CCAR-F Exam Guide — D2, Task 2.2

cards.front: Four MCP error categories the exam distinguishes?
cards.back: Transient (timeouts, unavailability), validation (invalid input), business (policy violations), permission (access denied).
sources: Official CCAR-F Exam Guide — D2, Task 2.2

cards.front: Why return generic 'Operation failed' for all tool errors?
cards.back: Prevents the agent from choosing appropriate recovery—retry, explain to user, escalate, or accept empty results.
sources: Official CCAR-F Exam Guide — D2, Task 2.2

cards.front: Structured error metadata fields for MCP tools (name three)?
cards.back: errorCategory (transient/validation/permission/business), isRetryable boolean, and human-readable description.
sources: Official CCAR-F Exam Guide — D2, Task 2.2

cards.front: Business rule violation (e.g., refund over policy limit). Error response design?
cards.back: isRetryable: false, customer-friendly explanation so the agent can communicate appropriately—not retry endlessly.
sources: Official CCAR-F Exam Guide — D2, Task 2.2

cards.front: Access failure (timeout) vs valid empty result (no matches)—how should tools report differently?
cards.back: Access failure: structured error with retry guidance. Valid empty: successful response indicating no matches—not an error.
sources: Official CCAR-F Exam Guide — D2, Task 2.2

cards.front: Transient failure in a subagent. Handle locally vs propagate to coordinator?
cards.back: Retry locally when possible; propagate only unresolved errors with partial results and what was attempted.
sources: Official CCAR-F Exam Guide — D2, Task 2.2

cards.front: Tool returns ambiguous error from external API. Best tool-layer behavior?
cards.back: Structured error payload (category, message, retryable flag)—not raw stack traces or silent failure.
sources: Official CCAR-F Exam Guide — D2, Task 2.2

cards.front: Why giving an agent 18 tools instead of 4–5 hurts reliability?
cards.back: Increases decision complexity and degrades tool selection accuracy.
sources: Official CCAR-F Exam Guide — D2, Task 2.3

cards.front: Synthesis agent attempts web searches. Likely tool design issue?
cards.back: Agent has tools outside its specialization—scoped access should limit synthesis to synthesis-appropriate tools.
sources: Official CCAR-F Exam Guide — D2, Task 2.3

cards.front: What is scoped tool access for subagents?
cards.back: Each agent gets only tools for its role, plus limited cross-role tools for specific high-frequency needs.
sources: Official CCAR-F Exam Guide — D2, Task 2.3

cards.front: Three tool_choice configuration options on the Claude API?
cards.back: "auto" (model may return text), "any" (must call a tool), and forced selection {"type": "tool", "name": "..."}.
sources: Official CCAR-F Exam Guide — D2, Task 2.3; Appendix

cards.front: When use tool_choice: "any"?
cards.back: When you need guaranteed tool invocation instead of conversational text—e.g., unknown document type among multiple extraction schemas.
sources: Official CCAR-F Exam Guide — D2, Task 2.3

cards.front: Must run extract_metadata before enrichment tools. tool_choice approach?
cards.back: Force specific tool first with {"type": "tool", "name": "extract_metadata"}, then process enrichment in follow-up turns.
sources: Official CCAR-F Exam Guide — D2, Task 2.3

cards.front: Replace generic fetch_url with what kind of constrained tool?
cards.back: Purpose-specific tool like load_document that validates document URLs and rejects non-document URLs.
sources: Official CCAR-F Exam Guide — D2, Task 2.3

cards.front: Synthesis needs simple fact-checks often. Scoped cross-role tool pattern?
cards.back: Provide verify_fact for high-frequency simple lookups; route complex verification through coordinator to search agent.
sources: Official CCAR-F Exam Guide — D2, Task 2.3; D1 Sample Q9

cards.front: Refund tool should only run after verified identity. Tool design choice?
cards.back: Least privilege: narrow tool exposure or refund tool requiring verified session token from prior identity tool.
sources: Official CCAR-F Exam Guide — D2, Task 2.3; Customer Support scenario

cards.front: Project-level vs user-level MCP server configuration?
cards.back: Project .mcp.json for shared team tooling (version controlled); user ~/.claude.json for personal/experimental servers.
sources: Official CCAR-F Exam Guide — D2, Task 2.4

cards.front: Store GitHub token for team MCP server without committing secrets?
cards.back: Environment variable expansion in .mcp.json (e.g., ${GITHUB_TOKEN}) with secrets in env—not in the repo.
sources: Official CCAR-F Exam Guide — D2, Task 2.4

cards.front: When are MCP tools from multiple servers available to the agent?
cards.back: All configured servers are discovered at connection time—tools from all servers are available simultaneously.
sources: Official CCAR-F Exam Guide — D2, Task 2.4

cards.front: MCP resources vs MCP tools—when use resources?
cards.back: Resources expose content catalogs (issue summaries, doc hierarchies, DB schemas) to reduce exploratory tool calls.
sources: Official CCAR-F Exam Guide — D2, Task 2.4

cards.front: Agent prefers Grep over a more capable MCP search tool. Fix?
cards.back: Enhance MCP tool descriptions to explain capabilities and outputs in detail so the model understands when MCP beats built-ins.
sources: Official CCAR-F Exam Guide — D2, Task 2.4

cards.front: Jira integration needed. Community MCP server vs custom?
cards.back: Prefer existing community MCP for standard integrations (Jira); custom servers for team-specific workflows.
sources: Official CCAR-F Exam Guide — D2, Task 2.4

cards.front: Built-in Claude Code tools vs custom MCP—when prefer MCP?
cards.back: MCP for external systems (GitHub, DB, SaaS) or sharing tools across clients; built-ins for local repo operations.
sources: Official CCAR-F Exam Guide — D2, Task 2.4–2.5

cards.front: Built-in Grep vs Glob—primary use case for each?
cards.back: Grep: search file contents for patterns (function names, errors, imports). Glob: match file paths by name/extension patterns.
sources: Official CCAR-F Exam Guide — D2, Task 2.5

cards.front: Find all test files named *.test.tsx anywhere in the repo. Which built-in tool?
cards.back: Glob with pattern like **/*.test.tsx.
sources: Official CCAR-F Exam Guide — D2, Task 2.5

cards.front: Find all callers of a function across the codebase. Which built-in tool?
cards.back: Grep to search file contents for the function name/reference patterns.
sources: Official CCAR-F Exam Guide — D2, Task 2.5

cards.front: Read/Write/Edit—when use Edit vs Read + Write?
cards.back: Edit for targeted changes with unique anchor text; Read + Write when Edit fails due to non-unique matches.
sources: Official CCAR-F Exam Guide — D2, Task 2.5

cards.front: Best incremental codebase exploration pattern?
cards.back: Grep for entry points → Read to follow imports and trace flows—not read all files upfront.
sources: Official CCAR-F Exam Guide — D2, Task 2.5

cards.front: Trace usage across wrapper modules exporting many names?
cards.back: Identify all exported names first, then Grep for each name across the codebase.
sources: Official CCAR-F Exam Guide — D2, Task 2.5

cards.front: Which three exam scenarios list D2 as a primary domain?
cards.back: Customer Support, Multi-Agent Research, and Developer Productivity.
sources: Official CCAR-F Exam Guide — scenario map

cards.front: Customer Support scenario MCP tools (Exam Scenario 1)—examples?
cards.back: get_customer, lookup_order, process_refund, escalate_to_human—backend integration via custom MCP tools.
sources: Official CCAR-F Exam Guide — Scenario 1

cards.front: Developer Productivity scenario built-in tools (Exam Scenario 4)?
cards.back: Read, Write, Bash, Grep, Glob—plus MCP server integrations for external systems.
sources: Official CCAR-F Exam Guide — Scenario 4

cards.front: Improve tool selection with keyword routing layer parsing user input each turn. Why often wrong?
cards.back: Over-engineered—bypasses LLM NLU; fix descriptions first; routing doesn't solve ordering or description gaps.
sources: Official CCAR-F Exam Guide — D2, Task 2.1; Sample Q2

cards.front: MCP tools vs MCP resources—division of responsibility?
cards.back: Tools perform actions (fetch, update, search); resources expose catalogs and static context (schemas, doc trees) to cut exploratory calls.
sources: Official CCAR-F Exam Guide — D2, Task 2.4; Appendix in-scope

cards.front: Why return structured isRetryable metadata on errors?
cards.back: Lets the agent retry transient failures and avoid wasted retries on non-retryable business or validation errors.
sources: Official CCAR-F Exam Guide — D2, Task 2.2

cards.front: What is CLAUDE.md in Claude Code workflows?
cards.back: Project instructions and context Claude Code loads to align behavior, conventions, and constraints.
sources: Official CCAR-F Exam Guide — D3, Task 3.1
https://docs.anthropic.com/en/docs/claude-code/overview

cards.front: CLAUDE.md configuration hierarchy (three levels)?
cards.back: User (~/.claude/CLAUDE.md), project (.claude/CLAUDE.md or root CLAUDE.md), and directory-level (subdirectory CLAUDE.md files).
sources: Official CCAR-F Exam Guide — D3, Task 3.1

cards.front: New teammate doesn't receive team coding standards in Claude Code. Likely cause?
cards.back: Instructions are in user-level ~/.claude/CLAUDE.md—not shared via version control; move to project-level config.
sources: Official CCAR-F Exam Guide — D3, Task 3.1

cards.front: What is @import syntax in CLAUDE.md?
cards.back: References external files to keep CLAUDE.md modular—import standards files relevant to each package.
sources: Official CCAR-F Exam Guide — D3, Task 3.1

cards.front: Monolithic CLAUDE.md is hard to maintain. Alternative organization?
cards.back: Split into focused files in .claude/rules/ (e.g., testing.md, api-conventions.md, deployment.md).
sources: Official CCAR-F Exam Guide — D3, Task 3.1

cards.front: Inconsistent Claude Code behavior across sessions—how diagnose loaded config?
cards.back: Use /memory to verify which memory files are loaded and what context is active.
sources: Official CCAR-F Exam Guide — D3, Task 3.1

cards.front: Why skip shared project CLAUDE.md when multiple developers use Claude Code?
cards.back: Inconsistent conventions, duplicated prompt context, and drift in how the agent edits code across teammates.
sources: Official CCAR-F Exam Guide — D3, Task 3.1

cards.front: Team /review slash command for every developer on clone. Where create it?
cards.back: .claude/commands/ in the project repository—version-controlled and shared on clone/pull.
sources: Official CCAR-F Exam Guide — D3, Task 3.2; Sample Q4

cards.front: Project-scoped vs user-scoped slash commands?
cards.back: .claude/commands/ in repo (shared via git) vs ~/.claude/commands/ (personal, not version controlled).
sources: Official CCAR-F Exam Guide — D3, Task 3.2

cards.front: Skill frontmatter options in .claude/skills/SKILL.md (name three)?
cards.back: context: fork, allowed-tools, and argument-hint.
sources: Official CCAR-F Exam Guide — D3, Task 3.2

cards.front: Skill produces verbose codebase analysis output. Frontmatter to isolate it?
cards.back: context: fork—runs skill in isolated sub-agent context so output doesn't pollute main conversation.
sources: Official CCAR-F Exam Guide — D3, Task 3.2

cards.front: Skill should only write files, not run destructive shell commands. Frontmatter?
cards.back: allowed-tools restricting tool access during skill execution (e.g., file write operations only).
sources: Official CCAR-F Exam Guide — D3, Task 3.2

cards.front: Developer invokes skill without required arguments. Frontmatter help?
cards.back: argument-hint prompts for required parameters when the skill is invoked without them.
sources: Official CCAR-F Exam Guide — D3, Task 3.2

cards.front: Skills vs CLAUDE.md—when use each?
cards.back: Skills: on-demand task-specific workflows. CLAUDE.md: always-loaded universal standards for the project.
sources: Official CCAR-F Exam Guide — D3, Task 3.2

cards.front: Personal skill customization without affecting teammates?
cards.back: Create personal variants in ~/.claude/skills/ with different names—not in shared project skills.
sources: Official CCAR-F Exam Guide — D3, Task 3.2

cards.front: How do .claude/rules/ path-specific rules activate?
cards.back: YAML frontmatter paths field with glob patterns—rules load only when editing matching files.
sources: Official CCAR-F Exam Guide — D3, Task 3.3

cards.front: Test files spread as Button.test.tsx next to Button.tsx. Apply test conventions automatically?
cards.back: .claude/rules/ with glob paths like **/*.test.tsx—applies by file type across all directories.
sources: Official CCAR-F Exam Guide — D3, Task 3.3; Sample Q6

cards.front: React, API, and DB areas need different conventions; tests scattered everywhere. Best maintainable approach?
cards.back: .claude/rules/ with YAML frontmatter glob patterns (e.g., paths: ["**/*.test.tsx"], ["src/api/**/*"])—not inference from one monolithic CLAUDE.md.
sources: Official CCAR-F Exam Guide — D3, Task 3.3; Sample Q6

cards.front: Path-specific rules vs subdirectory CLAUDE.md for scattered test files?
cards.back: Path-specific glob rules apply by file pattern anywhere in the tree; subdirectory CLAUDE.md is directory-bound.
sources: Official CCAR-F Exam Guide — D3, Task 3.3

cards.front: Benefit of path-scoped rules loading only on matching files?
cards.back: Reduces irrelevant context and token usage—conventions apply only when relevant.
sources: Official CCAR-F Exam Guide — D3, Task 3.3

cards.front: Restructure monolith into microservices—dozens of files, architectural decisions. Approach?
cards.back: Plan mode: explore codebase, understand dependencies, design approach before making changes.
sources: Official CCAR-F Exam Guide — D3, Task 3.4; Sample Q5

cards.front: Plan mode vs direct execution—when use each?
cards.back: Plan mode: large-scale, multi-file, architectural, multiple valid approaches. Direct execution: simple, well-scoped single changes.
sources: Official CCAR-F Exam Guide — D3, Task 3.4

cards.front: Single-file bug fix with clear stack trace. Plan mode or direct execution?
cards.back: Direct execution—well-understood change with clear scope.
sources: Official CCAR-F Exam Guide — D3, Task 3.4

cards.front: What is the Explore subagent used for in Claude Code?
cards.back: Isolates verbose discovery output and returns summaries—preserves main conversation context during exploration.
sources: Official CCAR-F Exam Guide — D3, Task 3.4

cards.front: Library migration affecting 45+ files—workflow pattern?
cards.back: Plan mode for investigation and design, then direct execution to implement the planned approach.
sources: Official CCAR-F Exam Guide — D3, Task 3.4

cards.front: Start monolith-to-microservices in direct execution, switch to plan if complexity emerges. Why wrong?
cards.back: Complexity is already stated—plan first prevents costly rework from late-discovered dependencies.
sources: Official CCAR-F Exam Guide — D3, Task 3.4; Sample Q5

cards.front: Natural language transformation spec produces inconsistent code. Best fix?
cards.back: Provide 2–3 concrete input/output examples showing expected transformations.
sources: Official CCAR-F Exam Guide — D3, Task 3.5

cards.front: Test-driven iteration pattern with Claude Code?
cards.back: Write tests first (behavior, edge cases, performance), then iterate by sharing test failures to guide fixes.
sources: Official CCAR-F Exam Guide — D3, Task 3.5

cards.front: What is the interview pattern in Claude Code workflows?
cards.back: Have Claude ask clarifying questions to surface design considerations before implementing in unfamiliar domains.
sources: Official CCAR-F Exam Guide — D3, Task 3.5

cards.front: Fix multiple issues in one message vs sequentially?
cards.back: Single message when fixes interact; sequential iteration when issues are independent.
sources: Official CCAR-F Exam Guide — D3, Task 3.5

cards.front: Migration script mishandles null edge cases. Iteration approach?
cards.back: Provide specific test cases with example input and expected output for the failing edge case.
sources: Official CCAR-F Exam Guide — D3, Task 3.5

cards.front: CI job hangs—Claude Code waiting for interactive input. Fix?
cards.back: Use -p (or --print) flag for non-interactive mode: process prompt, output result, exit.
sources: Official CCAR-F Exam Guide — D3, Task 3.6; Sample Q10

cards.front: Post structured PR review findings as inline comments from CI. CLI flags?
cards.back: --output-format json with --json-schema for machine-parseable structured findings.
sources: Official CCAR-F Exam Guide — D3, Task 3.6

cards.front: How provide project context to CI-invoked Claude Code?
cards.back: CLAUDE.md with testing standards, fixture conventions, and review criteria loaded automatically.
sources: Official CCAR-F Exam Guide — D3, Task 3.6

cards.front: Why use an independent Claude instance to review code it generated in the same session?
cards.back: Session context isolation—generator retains reasoning context and is less likely to question its own decisions.
sources: Official CCAR-F Exam Guide — D3, Task 3.6

cards.front: Re-run PR review after new commits—avoid duplicate inline comments?
cards.back: Include prior review findings in context; instruct Claude to report only new or still-unaddressed issues.
sources: Official CCAR-F Exam Guide — D3, Task 3.6

cards.front: CI test generation suggests scenarios already in the suite. Context fix?
cards.back: Provide existing test files in context so generation avoids duplicate coverage.
sources: Official CCAR-F Exam Guide — D3, Task 3.6

cards.front: Reduce low-value generated tests in Claude Code?
cards.back: Document testing standards, valuable test criteria, and available fixtures in CLAUDE.md.
sources: Official CCAR-F Exam Guide — D3, Task 3.6

cards.front: Running Claude Code in CI for PR review. Critical configuration concerns?
cards.back: Non-interactive (-p), explicit permissions, structured/deterministic outputs, independent review instance—not open-ended agent runs.
sources: Official CCAR-F Exam Guide — D3, Task 3.6

cards.front: CI non-interactive flags that do NOT exist (name two)?
cards.back: CLAUDE_HEADLESS env var and --batch flag—use -p/--print instead.
sources: Official CCAR-F Exam Guide — D3, Task 3.6; Sample Q10

cards.front: Code Generation scenario (Scenario 2)—primary domains?
cards.back: D3 (Claude Code config/workflows) and D5 (context management/reliability).
sources: Official CCAR-F Exam Guide — scenario map

cards.front: CI/CD with Claude Code scenario (Scenario 5)—primary domains?
cards.back: D3 (Claude Code) and D4 (prompt engineering/structured output for review findings).
sources: Official CCAR-F Exam Guide — scenario map

cards.front: Scenario 2 tools: slash commands, CLAUDE.md, plan mode—what is being tested?
cards.back: Integrating Claude Code into dev workflow: team config, custom commands, and when to plan vs execute directly.
sources: Official CCAR-F Exam Guide — Scenario 2

cards.front: Example path-scoped rule for Terraform files only?
cards.back: .claude/rules/ file with frontmatter paths: ["terraform/**/*"] loading only when editing matching files.
sources: Official CCAR-F Exam Guide — D3, Task 3.3

cards.front: Put all area conventions in root CLAUDE.md headers—rely on Claude to infer which applies. Why unreliable?
cards.back: Relies on inference vs explicit path matching—rules with glob patterns give deterministic automatic application.
sources: Official CCAR-F Exam Guide — D3, Task 3.3; Sample Q6

cards.front: Why use structured output (JSON schema) instead of parsing free-text responses?
cards.back: Enables validation, automated retries on failure, and downstream automation without fragile regex on prose.
sources: Official CCAR-F Exam Guide — D4, Task 4.3
https://docs.anthropic.com/en/docs/build-with-claude/structured-outputs

cards.front: Explicit review criteria vs vague instructions like 'be conservative'?
cards.back: Specific categorical criteria (flag when comment contradicts code) beat vague confidence filtering for precision.
sources: Official CCAR-F Exam Guide — D4, Task 4.1

cards.front: Automated review has high false positives in one category—developers ignore all findings. First response?
cards.back: Temporarily disable the high false-positive category to restore trust while improving prompts for that category.
sources: Official CCAR-F Exam Guide — D4, Task 4.1

cards.front: How define consistent severity levels in automated code review prompts?
cards.back: Explicit severity criteria with concrete code examples for each level—not generic confidence thresholds.
sources: Official CCAR-F Exam Guide — D4, Task 4.1

cards.front: Why high false-positive rates in one review category hurt the whole system?
cards.back: Developers lose trust and dismiss accurate findings in other categories too.
sources: Official CCAR-F Exam Guide — D4, Task 4.1

cards.front: Review prompt design: report bugs/security vs skip minor style?
cards.back: Define explicit categories to report versus skip—don't rely on confidence-based filtering alone.
sources: Official CCAR-F Exam Guide — D4, Task 4.1

cards.front: When are few-shot examples most effective?
cards.back: When detailed instructions alone produce inconsistent format or ambiguous-case handling—enables generalization to novel patterns.
sources: Official CCAR-F Exam Guide — D4, Task 4.2

cards.front: Review output format inconsistent (location, severity, fix). Improvement?
cards.back: Few-shot examples demonstrating exact desired format (location, issue, severity, suggested fix).
sources: Official CCAR-F Exam Guide — D4, Task 4.2

cards.front: Reduce false positives while still catching real bugs in review?
cards.back: Few-shot examples distinguishing acceptable local patterns from genuine issues—shows reasoning for each.
sources: Official CCAR-F Exam Guide — D4, Task 4.2

cards.front: Extraction fails on varied document layouts (inline citations vs bibliographies). Fix?
cards.back: Few-shot examples showing correct handling of each document structure variant.
sources: Official CCAR-F Exam Guide — D4, Task 4.2

cards.front: Model returns null/empty for required fields on varied formats. Few-shot approach?
cards.back: Examples demonstrating correct extraction from each format variant—not just schema tightening alone.
sources: Official CCAR-F Exam Guide — D4, Task 4.2

cards.front: How many few-shot examples for ambiguous scenarios, and what show?
cards.back: 2–4 targeted examples with reasoning for why one action was chosen over plausible alternatives.
sources: Official CCAR-F Exam Guide — D4, Task 4.2

cards.front: Most reliable approach for guaranteed schema-compliant JSON output?
cards.back: tool_use with JSON schemas—eliminates JSON syntax errors vs free-text JSON generation.
sources: Official CCAR-F Exam Guide — D4, Task 4.3

cards.front: Strict JSON schemas via tool_use eliminate syntax errors—but what errors remain?
cards.back: Semantic errors: wrong field values, line items not summing to total, values in incorrect fields.
sources: Official CCAR-F Exam Guide — D4, Task 4.3–4.4

cards.front: Source document may omit a field. Schema design to prevent fabrication?
cards.back: Make fields optional/nullable when information may be absent—don't require fields the source lacks.
sources: Official CCAR-F Exam Guide — D4, Task 4.3

cards.front: Extensible category field in extraction schema—pattern?
cards.back: Enum with "other" plus a detail string field for categories not in the predefined list.
sources: Official CCAR-F Exam Guide — D4, Task 4.3

cards.front: Ambiguous source data in extraction—enum design?
cards.back: Add enum value like "unclear" for ambiguous cases rather than forcing a wrong category.
sources: Official CCAR-F Exam Guide — D4, Task 4.3

cards.front: Inconsistent date formats in source documents alongside strict schema?
cards.back: Include format normalization rules in the prompt alongside the strict output schema.
sources: Official CCAR-F Exam Guide — D4, Task 4.3

cards.front: Multiple extraction schemas; document type unknown at request time. tool_choice?
cards.back: tool_choice: "any" to guarantee structured tool output instead of conversational text.
sources: Official CCAR-F Exam Guide — D4, Task 4.3

cards.front: Where extract structured data from a tool_use extraction call?
cards.back: From the tool_use response block—schema defines tool input parameters; model fills structured fields there.
sources: Official CCAR-F Exam Guide — D4, Task 4.3

cards.front: What is retry-with-error-feedback for extraction?
cards.back: On validation failure, send follow-up with original document, failed extraction, and specific validation errors for self-correction.
sources: Official CCAR-F Exam Guide — D4, Task 4.4

cards.front: When will validation retries succeed vs fail?
cards.back: Succeed on format/structural mismatches. Fail when required info is absent from source (or only in external doc not provided).
sources: Official CCAR-F Exam Guide — D4, Task 4.4

cards.front: Schema syntax errors vs semantic validation errors?
cards.back: Syntax errors eliminated by tool_use strict schemas; semantic errors need cross-field rules (totals, field placement).
sources: Official CCAR-F Exam Guide — D4, Task 4.4

cards.front: Developers dismiss many automated findings. Feedback loop design?
cards.back: Add detected_pattern field to findings to analyze which constructs trigger false positives when dismissed.
sources: Official CCAR-F Exam Guide — D4, Task 4.4

cards.front: Self-correction for invoice totals that don't add up?
cards.back: Extract calculated_total alongside stated_total and flag discrepancies; add conflict_detected for inconsistent source data.
sources: Official CCAR-F Exam Guide — D4, Task 4.4

cards.front: Extraction misses nullable fields intermittently. Best improvement?
cards.back: Tighten required vs optional schema, validation-retry loop, and explicit examples for null/edge cases.
sources: Official CCAR-F Exam Guide — D4, Task 4.3–4.4; Structured Extraction scenario

cards.front: Message Batches API tradeoffs (cost, latency)?
cards.back: 50% cost savings, up to 24-hour processing window, no guaranteed latency SLA.
sources: Official CCAR-F Exam Guide — D4, Task 4.5; Appendix

cards.front: Pre-merge blocking check vs overnight technical debt report—batch API for both?
cards.back: Batch only for latency-tolerant jobs (overnight reports); keep synchronous API for blocking pre-merge checks.
sources: Official CCAR-F Exam Guide — D4, Task 4.5; Sample Q11

cards.front: Message Batches API limitation on tool calling?
cards.back: No multi-turn tool calling within a single batch request—cannot execute tools mid-request and return results.
sources: Official CCAR-F Exam Guide — D4, Task 4.5

cards.front: custom_id in Message Batches API—purpose?
cards.back: Correlate batch request/response pairs and identify failed documents for resubmission.
sources: Official CCAR-F Exam Guide — D4, Task 4.5

cards.front: Batch job failures—resubmission strategy?
cards.back: Resubmit only failed documents by custom_id with modifications (e.g., chunk oversized docs that exceeded context).
sources: Official CCAR-F Exam Guide — D4, Task 4.5

cards.front: Before batch-processing 10,000 documents—cost reduction step?
cards.back: Refine prompts on a sample set first to maximize first-pass success and reduce resubmission costs.
sources: Official CCAR-F Exam Guide — D4, Task 4.5

cards.front: Why self-review of generated code in the same session is limited?
cards.back: Model retains generation reasoning context—less likely to question its own decisions than an independent reviewer.
sources: Official CCAR-F Exam Guide — D4, Task 4.6

cards.front: Best approach to catch subtle issues in AI-generated code?
cards.back: Second independent Claude instance reviewing without the generator's reasoning context.
sources: Official CCAR-F Exam Guide — D4, Task 4.6

cards.front: Large multi-file PR review—multi-pass architecture?
cards.back: Per-file passes for local issues plus separate integration pass for cross-file data flow.
sources: Official CCAR-F Exam Guide — D4, Task 4.6; Sample Q12

cards.front: Route review findings to human triage by severity—schema approach?
cards.back: Verification pass where model reports confidence alongside each finding for calibrated routing.
sources: Official CCAR-F Exam Guide — D4, Task 4.6

cards.front: Prompt-only PR findings vs JSON schema for CI gates?
cards.back: Schema for machine consumption (CI gates, dashboards); prompts alone only for human-readable narrative.
sources: Official CCAR-F Exam Guide — D4, Task 4.3; CI/CD scenario

cards.front: Why trust model self-reported confidence without validation?
cards.back: Not calibrated by default—use schema checks, cross-field rules, or human review thresholds for high-risk fields.
sources: Official CCAR-F Exam Guide — D4, Task 4.4; D5 crossover

cards.front: Run three full PR review passes and only flag issues in 2+ passes. Why wrong?
cards.back: Suppresses real bugs caught intermittently—consensus filtering hides attention-dilution problems; split passes instead.
sources: Official CCAR-F Exam Guide — D4, Task 4.6; Sample Q12

cards.front: Structured Data Extraction scenario (Scenario 6)—primary domains?
cards.back: D4 (schemas, validation, batch) and D5 (reliability, human review for low confidence).
sources: Official CCAR-F Exam Guide — scenario map

cards.front: Scenario 6 extraction system requirements from the exam guide?
cards.back: Extract from unstructured docs, validate with JSON schemas, handle edge cases, integrate with downstream systems.
sources: Official CCAR-F Exam Guide — Scenario 6

cards.front: Few-shot examples reduce hallucination in extraction—example use cases?
cards.back: Informal measurements, varied document structures, and inconsistent field formats in source documents.
sources: Official CCAR-F Exam Guide — D4, Task 4.2

cards.front: Switch blocking pre-merge checks to batch API with status polling. Why wrong?
cards.back: Batch has no latency SLA—unacceptable for workflows where developers wait to merge.
sources: Official CCAR-F Exam Guide — D4, Task 4.5; Sample Q11

cards.front: 30-hour SLA with 24-hour max batch processing—submission frequency?
cards.back: Calculate submission windows (e.g., 4-hour intervals) so batches complete within SLA with margin for retries.
sources: Official CCAR-F Exam Guide — D4, Task 4.5

cards.front: Independent review instances vs extended thinking for self-review?
cards.back: Independent instances without generator context catch more subtle issues than self-review instructions or extended thinking alone.
sources: Official CCAR-F Exam Guide — D4, Task 4.6

cards.front: What is context degradation in long agent sessions?
cards.back: Reasoning quality drops as irrelevant history accumulates—inconsistent answers and vague 'typical pattern' references instead of specifics.
sources: Official CCAR-F Exam Guide — D5, Task 5.4

cards.front: Risk of progressive summarization in long support sessions?
cards.back: Condenses amounts, dates, percentages, and customer-stated expectations into vague summaries—loses critical transactional facts.
sources: Official CCAR-F Exam Guide — D5, Task 5.1

cards.front: What is the 'lost in the middle' effect?
cards.back: Models reliably use info at the start and end of long inputs but may omit findings buried in middle sections.
sources: Official CCAR-F Exam Guide — D5, Task 5.1

cards.front: Preserve order amounts and dates across a long support conversation?
cards.back: Extract transactional facts into a persistent case facts block in each prompt—outside summarized history.
sources: Official CCAR-F Exam Guide — D5, Task 5.1

cards.front: Order lookup returns 40+ fields but only 5 matter for returns. Context fix?
cards.back: Trim verbose tool outputs to relevant fields before they accumulate in conversation context.
sources: Official CCAR-F Exam Guide — D5, Task 5.1

cards.front: Mitigate lost-in-the-middle when aggregating subagent results?
cards.back: Place key findings summary at the beginning; organize detailed results with explicit section headers.
sources: Official CCAR-F Exam Guide — D5, Task 5.1

cards.front: Downstream synthesis agent has limited context budget. Upstream agent output design?
cards.back: Return structured key facts, citations, and relevance scores—not verbose reasoning chains.
sources: Official CCAR-F Exam Guide — D5, Task 5.1

cards.front: Why pass complete conversation history in subsequent API requests?
cards.back: Maintains conversational coherence—the model needs prior turns to reason about the ongoing case.
sources: Official CCAR-F Exam Guide — D5, Task 5.1

cards.front: Multi-issue support session (billing + return). Context layer approach?
cards.back: Persist structured issue data (order IDs, amounts, statuses) in a separate context layer for each concern.
sources: Official CCAR-F Exam Guide — D5, Task 5.1

cards.front: Three appropriate escalation triggers (beyond 'complex case')?
cards.back: Customer explicitly requests human, policy exception/gap, and inability to make meaningful progress.
sources: Official CCAR-F Exam Guide — D5, Task 5.2

cards.front: 55% FCR—escalates easy cases, handles hard policy exceptions alone. Best calibration fix?
cards.back: Add explicit escalation criteria with few-shot examples showing escalate vs resolve autonomously.
sources: Official CCAR-F Exam Guide — D5, Task 5.2; Sample Q3

cards.front: Route to human when self-reported confidence score is below threshold. Why unreliable?
cards.back: LLM confidence is poorly calibrated—agent may be wrongly confident on hard cases and uncertain on easy ones.
sources: Official CCAR-F Exam Guide — D5, Task 5.2; Sample Q3

cards.front: Escalate on negative sentiment threshold. Why wrong for calibration?
cards.back: Sentiment doesn't correlate with case complexity—the actual issue is unclear escalation boundaries.
sources: Official CCAR-F Exam Guide — D5, Task 5.2; Sample Q3

cards.front: Customer explicitly demands a human agent. Response?
cards.back: Honor immediately—do not attempt investigation first when they explicitly request a human.
sources: Official CCAR-F Exam Guide — D5, Task 5.2

cards.front: Frustrated customer, issue is within agent capability. Approach?
cards.back: Acknowledge frustration and offer resolution; escalate only if customer reiterates preference for human.
sources: Official CCAR-F Exam Guide — D5, Task 5.2

cards.front: Policy silent on competitor price matching (only covers own-site adjustments). Action?
cards.back: Escalate—policy gap/exception case, not autonomous resolution.
sources: Official CCAR-F Exam Guide — D5, Task 5.2

cards.front: get_customer returns multiple matches. What should the agent do?
cards.back: Ask for additional identifiers—never pick a match heuristically.
sources: Official CCAR-F Exam Guide — D5, Task 5.2

cards.front: Subagents need prior search results. Best context passing?
cards.back: Explicit structured handoffs (IDs, snippets, citations) via coordinator—not implicit shared memory.
sources: Official CCAR-F Exam Guide — D5, Task 5.1; Multi-Agent Research scenario

cards.front: Web search subagent timeout—best error propagation to coordinator?
cards.back: Structured context: failure type, attempted query, partial results, and alternative approaches.
sources: Official CCAR-F Exam Guide — D5, Task 5.3; Sample Q8

cards.front: Subagent returns empty results marked successful after timeout. Why anti-pattern?
cards.back: Silently suppresses errors—coordinator cannot recover or annotate coverage gaps.
sources: Official CCAR-F Exam Guide — D5, Task 5.3; Sample Q8

cards.front: Synthesis output after partial subagent failures—what include?
cards.back: Coverage annotations: which findings are well-supported vs which topic areas have gaps from unavailable sources.
sources: Official CCAR-F Exam Guide — D5, Task 5.3

cards.front: Agent loop fails twice on same tool error. Next step?
cards.back: Escalate or change strategy (alternate tool, human handoff)—not infinite identical retries.
sources: Official CCAR-F Exam Guide — D5, Task 5.3

cards.front: Scratchpad files in long Claude Code exploration sessions—purpose?
cards.back: Persist key findings across context boundaries; reference for later questions to counteract degradation.
sources: Official CCAR-F Exam Guide — D5, Task 5.4

cards.front: Verbose codebase exploration fills context. Claude Code command to reduce usage?
cards.back: /compact to condense verbose discovery output during extended sessions.
sources: Official CCAR-F Exam Guide — D5, Task 5.4; Appendix

cards.front: Multi-phase codebase exploration—context pattern between phases?
cards.back: Summarize key findings from one phase, inject summary into context before spawning subagents for the next.
sources: Official CCAR-F Exam Guide — D5, Task 5.4

cards.front: Crash recovery pattern for multi-agent workflows?
cards.back: Each agent exports state to a known location; coordinator loads manifest on resume and injects into prompts.
sources: Official CCAR-F Exam Guide — D5, Task 5.4

cards.front: Why dump entire repo into context for every Claude Code task?
cards.back: Wastes tokens and adds noise—use Grep/Glob and scoped reads incrementally.
sources: Official CCAR-F Exam Guide — D5, Task 5.4; D2 Task 2.5

cards.front: 97% overall extraction accuracy—why not automate all human review?
cards.back: Aggregate metrics may mask poor performance on specific document types or individual fields.
sources: Official CCAR-F Exam Guide — D5, Task 5.5

cards.front: Ongoing quality monitoring for high-confidence extractions?
cards.back: Stratified random sampling to measure error rates and detect novel error patterns.
sources: Official CCAR-F Exam Guide — D5, Task 5.5

cards.front: Calibrate human review routing for extractions?
cards.back: Model outputs field-level confidence; calibrate thresholds using labeled validation sets.
sources: Official CCAR-F Exam Guide — D5, Task 5.5

cards.front: Before reducing human review on high-confidence extractions—verify what?
cards.back: Accuracy by document type and field segment—consistent performance across all segments.
sources: Official CCAR-F Exam Guide — D5, Task 5.5

cards.front: Limited reviewer capacity—prioritize which extractions for human review?
cards.back: Low model confidence, ambiguous source documents, or contradictory source data.
sources: Official CCAR-F Exam Guide — D5, Task 5.5

cards.front: How is source attribution lost in multi-agent research pipelines?
cards.back: Summarization compresses findings without preserving claim-to-source mappings.
sources: Official CCAR-F Exam Guide — D5, Task 5.6

cards.front: Subagent output for downstream synthesis—provenance requirement?
cards.back: Structured claim-source mappings (URLs, document names, excerpts) preserved through synthesis.
sources: Official CCAR-F Exam Guide — D5, Task 5.6

cards.front: Two credible sources report different statistics. Synthesis handling?
cards.back: Annotate conflict with source attribution—do not arbitrarily pick one value.
sources: Official CCAR-F Exam Guide — D5, Task 5.6

cards.front: Why require publication/collection dates in structured subagent outputs?
cards.back: Enables correct temporal interpretation—prevents time differences being misread as contradictions.
sources: Official CCAR-F Exam Guide — D5, Task 5.6

cards.front: Research report structure for contested vs established findings?
cards.back: Explicit sections distinguishing well-established findings from contested ones with methodological context.
sources: Official CCAR-F Exam Guide — D5, Task 5.6

cards.front: Synthesis output formatting for mixed content types?
cards.back: Render appropriately—financial data as tables, news as prose, technical findings as structured lists.
sources: Official CCAR-F Exam Guide — D5, Task 5.6

cards.front: Which three scenarios list D5 as a primary domain?
cards.back: Customer Support, Multi-Agent Research, and Structured Data Extraction.
sources: Official CCAR-F Exam Guide — scenario map

cards.front: Code Generation scenario (Scenario 2)—D5 focus areas?
cards.back: Context preservation across edits, plan vs execute context management, and session reliability.
sources: Official CCAR-F Exam Guide — Scenario 2

cards.front: What is the official exam code for Claude Certified Architect, Foundations?
cards.back: CCAR-F (also written CCA-F or CCAF in older materials).
cards.rationale: Pearson lists CCAR-F as the current code.
sources: Official CCAR-F Exam Guide
https://docs.anthropic.com/en/docs/about-claude/models

cards.front: CCAR-F format: how many questions, time limit, and passing score?
cards.back: 60 scenario-based items, 120 minutes, pass at scaled 720 on a 100–1000 scale.
sources: Official CCAR-F Exam Guide

cards.front: How many scenarios appear on the exam, and from what pool?
cards.back: 4 scenarios per exam, drawn randomly from a published bank of 6.
sources: Official CCAR-F Exam Guide

cards.front: Core heuristic when a scenario needs deterministic guarantees (money, identity, schema compliance)?
cards.back: Prefer structural/programmatic fixes (hooks, prerequisites, scoped tools, tool_use schemas) over prompt-only instructions.
cards.rationale: Exam tests judgment: prompts are insufficient for hard guarantees.
sources: Community study guides aligned to Exam Guide patterns
